questions: I find it difficult to stay focused on tasks that do not hold my interest.
I often intend to do something but struggle to get started, even when it is important.
I frequently lose track of what I was doing when my attention is interrupted.
Organising everyday tasks, priorities or deadlines takes considerable effort for me.
I sometimes act or speak before I have had time to think through the consequences.
I find it uncomfortable to remain inactive when I feel the need to be doing something.
I am easily drawn towards something new or interesting, even when I should be concentrating on something else.
I sometimes have difficulty working out what another person expects from me when they do not say it directly.
Social situations often require conscious effort rather than feeling automatic.
I sometimes realise afterwards that I misunderstood another person's tone, intention or reaction.
I find conversations involving unspoken social rules harder to navigate than conversations with a clear purpose.
Certain sounds, lights, textures, smells or other sensations affect me more strongly than they seem to affect other people.
Busy environments with many things happening at once can become overwhelming for me.
I sometimes avoid places, clothing, foods or activities because of how they feel to my senses.
Unexpected changes to plans can unsettle me more than I would like.
I feel more comfortable when I know what to expect and can prepare for it.
Once I have settled into a particular way of doing something, changing that approach can be difficult.
When something strongly interests me, I can become so absorbed that I lose awareness of time or other things I need to do.
Repetitive movements, sounds or familiar activities can help me regulate myself when I am stressed, restless or overwhelmed.
Switching my attention away from something I am deeply engaged in can be difficult, even when I know I need to stop.
I can strongly prefer predictability while also becoming restless or drawn towards novelty.
I sometimes feel pulled between needing structure to function well and resisting that same structure when it feels restrictive.
framing: Think about your usual experiences as an adult, across different parts of your life. Choose the answer that best reflects you overall.
There are no right or wrong answers. Try to answer based on what is generally true for you, rather than an unusual good or difficult day.
reassurances: Each question helps build a clearer picture of your traits.
Some questions may feel similar, but they explore different aspects of your experience.
Your responses are helping us understand how different traits may overlap.
You're making good progress. The remaining questions help complete your trait profile.
Nearly there. These final responses help complete the overall picture.

results.name: No strong trait pattern identified
results.text: Your responses did not show a strong overall pattern of ADHD-associated or ASD-associated traits in this assessment. You may still recognise individual traits in your results, but they were not prominent enough here to form a stronger overall pattern.

results.name: ADHD-associated traits
results.text: Your responses show a stronger pattern of traits commonly associated with ADHD, particularly in areas such as attention, executive function, impulsivity or activity regulation. This result is for self-reflection and does not establish an ADHD diagnosis.

results.name: ASD-associated traits
results.text: Your responses show a stronger pattern of traits commonly associated with autism, particularly in areas such as social communication, sensory processing, routine or predictability. This result is for self-reflection and does not establish an autism diagnosis.

results.name: AuDHD-associated traits
results.text: Your responses show a pattern of traits associated with both ADHD and autism. This combination is commonly referred to as AuDHD. This result is for self-reflection and does not establish an ADHD, autism or AuDHD diagnosis.

summaries.title: Your pattern looks relatively balanced
summaries.text: Your responses did not show a strong overall ADHD-associated or ASD-associated pattern. You may still recognise individual traits in some areas, and those can still be useful for understanding what helps or challenges you.

summaries.title: Notice the areas that stand out
summaries.text: Your detailed results may show particular Lower, Moderate or Higher areas even without a strong overall classification. Those individual patterns can be more useful than the overall label alone.

summaries.title: Use what is useful
summaries.text: If a particular difficulty affects your daily life, you can still explore practical strategies or discuss it with a qualified professional regardless of this result.

summaries.title: Attention may depend on interest and demand
summaries.text: Your responses suggest that directing attention, starting tasks or organising priorities may require more effort, particularly when something is repetitive or less engaging.

summaries.title: Regulation can vary by situation
summaries.text: Restlessness, impulsive responses or attraction to something more interesting may become more noticeable in some environments than others.

summaries.title: Strengths and challenges can coexist
summaries.text: The same patterns that make some tasks difficult may also accompany curiosity, energy or strong engagement when something captures your attention. Context matters.

summaries.title: Predictability can reduce effort
summaries.text: Your responses suggest that clear expectations, preparation or familiar ways of doing things may make some situations easier to navigate.

summaries.title: Sensory and social demands can matter
summaries.text: Your environment and the amount of interpretation required in social situations may affect your concentration, comfort or energy.

summaries.title: Strengths and challenges can coexist
summaries.text: The same traits can be useful in some settings and demanding in others. Understanding the environments that work well for you can be valuable.

summaries.title: Big ideas, different focus
summaries.text: You may experience periods of intense focus alongside difficulty directing your attention towards tasks that feel less engaging.

summaries.title: Sensory patterns matter
summaries.text: Sensitivity to your environment may affect concentration, energy and how easily you become overwhelmed.

summaries.title: Strengths and challenges can coexist
summaries.text: The same traits can be helpful in some situations and difficult in others. Context often makes a significant difference.

terms.title: Purpose of MindLens
paragraphs: MindLens is a research-informed self-assessment designed to help you reflect on traits associated with ADHD, Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and overlapping ADHD and ASD traits commonly referred to as AuDHD.

terms.title: Not a diagnosis or medical advice
paragraphs: MindLens is not a diagnostic instrument and does not replace assessment, diagnosis, treatment or advice from a qualified healthcare professional.

terms.title: Accuracy and limitations
paragraphs: Your results are based on your responses and research-informed screening concepts. They cannot establish whether you have ADHD, ASD, AuDHD or another condition. Other conditions, circumstances and life experiences may produce similar traits.

terms.title: Your results and decisions
paragraphs: MindLens results are provided for information and self-reflection. Any decisions you make after viewing your results remain your responsibility.

terms.title: Emergency situations
paragraphs: MindLens is not an emergency, crisis or medical service. If you require urgent help, contact the appropriate emergency or crisis service in your location.

terms.title: Professional support listings
paragraphs: Professional support listings are provided to help you locate institutional assessment services. Provider information may change. Always check the provider's website for current information.

terms.title: Personal information and assessment responses
paragraphs: MindLens does not require an account, name, email address or phone number to complete the assessment.

Your assessment results are not permanently stored by MindLens and are intended to remain available only during your current browser session. Standard hosting infrastructure may process technical information required to deliver the website.

terms.title: Limitation of liability
paragraphs: By using MindLens, you acknowledge that the assessment is provided for informational and self-reflection purposes only and is not a medical or clinical diagnosis.

To the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, MindLens, its creators, contributors and technical providers will not be liable for any loss, harm, distress, decision, action or consequence arising from your use of, or reliance on, the assessment, its results, recommendations, external links or listed support services.
You agree that you use MindLens voluntarily and at your own discretion and accept responsibility for any decisions you make based on the information provided.
Nothing in these Terms excludes or limits any rights or liabilities that cannot legally be excluded.

paragraphs: MindLens may change its assessment, content, functionality or these Terms as the product develops.

accuracyIntro: MindLens is a research-informed self-assessment designed to help you explore traits associated with ADHD, Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and AuDHD.

accuracy.title: What can the results tell me?
paragraphs: Your responses can highlight patterns commonly associated with ADHD, ASD or both, including areas such as attention, executive function, sensory processing, social communication and other overlapping traits.
The results can help you identify areas you may want to understand or explore further.

accuracy.title: What can't the results tell me?
paragraphs: MindLens cannot determine with certainty whether you have ADHD, ASD, AuDHD or another condition.

There is currently insufficient evidence to establish the diagnostic accuracy of a combined assessment like MindLens. Different conditions, circumstances and life experiences can also produce similar traits.
Your result is a guide for self-reflection, not a diagnosis.

accuracy.title: Research-informed, not diagnostic
paragraphs: MindLens draws on published research and established screening approaches for ADHD and autism.

Screening tools can help identify traits that may warrant further assessment, but they are not sufficient on their own to make a diagnosis. Professional assessment considers additional factors such as developmental history, everyday functioning, symptoms across different settings and alternative explanations.

accuracy.title: No paywall. No paid results.
paragraphs: MindLens is free to use. Your complete assessment and results are available without payment.
Optional donations help support hosting and maintenance.

accuracy.title: Your results are temporary
paragraphs: No account is required.
Your results are not saved by MindLens and are only available during your current session.

accuracy.title: Want greater certainty?
paragraphs: If your results raise questions or you would like greater clarity, consider discussing them with a qualified professional.

support.intro: MindLens is a free independent project created to make research-informed ADHD, ASD and AuDHD self-reflection more accessible.
body: Keeping MindLens free still has costs, including hosting, maintenance and continued development. If you find the project useful and would like to support it, an optional contribution helps me keep improving MindLens while keeping the assessment and results free for everyone.
There is no paid version, subscription or locked result. Supporting MindLens does not change what you can access.
